heldBackBy.answer: Being honest where it counted: the game seems to punish speaking up with STAND, and the ending card blames one Lo Hei answer at 43. I never understood what STAND measured, so I felt held back by a stat I couldn't read.

I suspect the low STAND from pushing the bottom 20th over and over, and from never being a safe pair of hands. The card says my party ceiling was Senior Minister of State, so I actually overshot it. Honestly I can't tell what held me back, because the game never explained STAND or COMP.

My guess is the favour I asked in Y1 and the blunt offsite note in Y2 together. But the ending says the scholarship mattered and my file didn't ever put a ceiling on me, which I didn't understand. I never had a scholarship, so it feels like something was decided before I started.

Honestly the game did: the politics step that every rumour promised never happened, so I retired as Perm Sec at 65 with the big payoff withheld. Possibly my STAND stayed too low for the invitation, or politics just wasn't reachable on this path.

Honestly, nothing held me back much. I reached Minister, past my estimated Deputy Secretary ceiling. If anything, asking outright in Cabinet and the early shortcuts cost me some STAND, but the game never showed me clearly what was driving it.
Mostly the party and the ward, not me: the card says it was never about me. My STAND stat sagged after I kept being honest and turning things down, so maybe I was too clean to be useful to anyone.

Honestly, nothing. The ending says my file had no ceiling, so it seems I just topped out at PS because there's nothing higher. The political invitation I kept waiting for never came, and I suspect STAND never got high enough, or the game just doesn't give it to you.
Mostly the STAND stat, which crashed after the Leak and never fully recovered, so I had great competence and integrity but little visibility. I suspect the game rewards being seen over being good.

Honestly, I think the game's hidden ceiling held me back more than anything I did. I started at Senior Director and only moved it with one choice at 45, and I never knew that was the lever. Asking about it directly backfired earlier.

The system had decided my ceiling early, and the party had its own lower estimate. Visible honesty kept costing me STAND, so I kept getting promotions that the ceiling then refused. I was good but never the kind of person they wanted at the top.

Mostly the game: I got a ceiling I wasn't told about, and the politics invitation I was waiting for never came. In-story, I think my public outspokenness (the Y35 and Y38 papers) kept my STAND low, so I stayed in the service.

I think I hit the top of the civil service and the only way up was politics, which the game kept hinting at and never offered. The STAND slide also seemed to drag with no cause shown, so I never learned what I could have done differently.

Honesty and speaking up kept costing me STAND with the establishment, even with outstanding appraisals and 100 integrity. I think the game rewards being likeable to the right people over being right, and I only found out about the ceiling at the end.

Mostly STAND, which I think is standing with my bosses, and my family choices probably dragged it down. The ending says the ceiling was never the problem and the party had already pegged me as Minister, so maybe nothing held me back and I just got where the game always meant me to go.

I think it was the system rather than me. The rumour was always that there was no rung above Permanent Secretary, and my STAND kept getting knocked down whenever I was honest or visible. The game seems to reward looking safe more than being right.

Mostly a hidden ceiling I was never told about. The service's estimate of me was Senior Director and the party's was Minister, and the rumours about not being on the list were the game hinting at it. My honest answers also kept costing STAND, so I think being straightforward kept me off the top.

A hidden ceiling in my file that I was never told about. The party and the civil service had both decided where I'd stop, and my candour kept my STAND low. I'm still not sure what STAND really measured.

Candour. Every time I said the awkward thing my STAND fell, while appraisals stayed strong. It looks like the system rewards the work but doesn't like colleagues who point out the rules. It didn't really hold me back in the end, though, because I became PM anyway.

Honestly, I think it was the invisible ceiling, not anything I did. I kept chasing politics, the Meet-the-People sessions, the networking and the nominations, but the invitation never came. The game seems to have decided my potential at the start and I only found out at the end.

Honesty, I think. The card says my blunt Y27 answer removed my ceiling, so being straight apparently capped me even though my appraisals always said strong. I also never got an invitation into politics, so maybe visibility mattered more than integrity.

Mostly the game: the politics rumour ran for over a decade and no approach ever came, and STAND drifted around without me understanding what moved it. My character was maxed on everything else, so the cap was in the design, not in my choices.

Probably the party's view of me, since I never got a portfolio. My STAND stayed lowish because I kept picking honesty and pushing hard, and it seems the game rewards being liked by the party over being right. I also don't fully understand how a MOS differs from a Minister here.

Mostly my own honesty, which cost me standing after the Leak and the fourth pillar. It still got me to the top, though, so nothing really held me back. I think the game just rewards honesty and I never felt a real trade-off.

I think it was STAND. I never got the visibility that politics needed, because my promotions kept lowering it and I was too blunt and too busy doing the work. The ceiling note says bluntness removed my ceiling in the service, so being honest probably made me un-politic. I'm guessing, since the game never explained it.

My STAND was low, and I think being honest and doing good work wasn't enough without being seen or well connected. I only became a Minister, and I never got near the top. I couldn't tell exactly what I was missing, which was frustrating.

Probably the hidden ceiling, which I only learned about at the end, plus low STAND with seniors. I was honest and did the work, but the game never made clear how to push past the ceiling, and politics never came.

Probably my low STAND. I was honest every time, which kept INTEG at 100 but cost me standing, and the game never gave the politics invitation. The ceiling was hidden too, so I could never tell whether it was STAND or the ceiling that stopped me.
Being candid cost me visibility, so my STAND stayed low while my integrity and competence maxed out. The game seems to reward being seen over being right, and I was right quietly.

Being blunt and tanking STAND, which the card says cost me my in-service ceiling, though I still reached Perm Sec and Minister. Honestly the party estimate of Senior Minister of State probably capped me from reaching Cabinet.

I think it was the low STAND, since candour kept costing me standing even though my integrity stayed at 100. The politics invitation never came, and the game never told me why, so I'm guessing. I may just have hit the top of the service, as the rumour said.

The file capped me at Deputy Secretary from the start, and my honesty cost me standing along the way. I never got to politics, and the card suggests the Counter choice took me outside the service's normal path. I still don't fully understand why I was stuck.

Probably my hidden ceiling, which was set early and only moved once, plus the slow STAND decline that I could not explain. I also never got invited into politics, so maybe the game wanted something from me that I never worked out.

Nothing I did, apparently. The ending says the ceiling was set before I joined and nothing I was offered could have changed it. That feels like the game saying my choices were decoration, which is a bit deflating. I also quit politics at 38 myself, so I may have capped my own climb.

Reputation. I was brilliant on paper (COMP 97) but REP stayed at 47 because I kept doing quiet, honest work nobody saw, and the political route seemed to need public recognition. I also suspect the team ticket meant my own results counted for less than the ward's.

Honestly nothing held me back, I got to PM. If anything the game held back the drama: honesty kept winning, so the stakes felt low. The rival, the credit-stealer, the Y13 board seat, the winking woman and the Y11 quote I flagged never came back, as far as I saw.

Me, mostly. I resigned my seat at 37 for a board seat that paid more, so I walked away from the Minister track the party had in mind. The game also seemed to reward gaming the system and then never charged me for it.

Honestly, the ending card says the ward result was never about me, so I think it was the party and the ward, not my choices. My REP was only 49 and I could not do much to raise it, so I wonder if that was the real cap. The card does not say.

Low STAND. I never worked out what it measures, and the ending says it was never about me. My guess is it tracks party or voter mood, not anything I did, so I couldn't fix it however honest or hard-working I was.

The ending card says nothing I did could have changed my ceiling, so it was the file and the party's estimate, not my choices. I got a perfect integrity score and 100 competence and still lost at 48.2%. That's a bit deflating if you play for ambition.

Nothing really held me back, I became Prime Minister. If anything the honest choices cost STAND, but it did not seem to matter. The card says my file never had a ceiling, so the game seemed to say the ceiling was set by one nomination choice rather than by my behaviour overall.

A hidden ceiling that was set by the party and my file, not by my work. Even with 100 rep, 100 integrity and outstanding appraisals, STAND kept sliding and the system had already decided where I would stop. I think challenging the pay system in Y42 cost me, too.

Mostly nothing. I got to PM at 59 with full integrity. The slow STAND slide late on, and starting with no ceiling in the file, were the only drag I could see. The game never told me what STAND was tied to.

A hidden ceiling in my file that the game never let me see or influence. I only learned at the end that STAND was linked to it, and the only thing that moved it was one choice at 46, which I picked almost at random.

Probably the party, not me. The card says they rated me Senior Minister of State, but I lost a seat on 48.2% after being honest and never saying 'team effort'. I suspect honesty raised my integrity but cost me standing, and the game never made clear which mattered at the ballot.

A hidden ceiling in my file and the party's low estimate of me, which I was never told about. My performance was outstanding and it did not matter until I asked for the hard ministry. Being straight with the public probably didn't help either.

Honestly I think the election decided it, not me. I took the single seat and lost, and the ending says it was never about me. Maybe the GRC team was the safer choice and I was never told. Retiring at 35 after the biggest gamble feels abrupt.

Honestly, me. I took the money at 33 and left. The card says my file never had a ceiling, so nothing else held me back. My REP was low at 40, though, and I suspect that is why no politics invitation came.

Every time I took the honest option my STAND dropped, so I think the game punishes integrity with political standing. The party's estimate of me was only Minister, and I was told that nobody told me. I never saw it, which makes it feel hidden rather than earned.

Low REP, which kept me from the single seat and probably sank the GRC vote, plus the fact that I got to Permanent Secretary at 32 and then had nowhere left to go inside the service. The card says my ceiling was never a limit, so the election seems to have been the real wall, and I did not understand how it worked.

skip.why: The salary committee submission was a lot of paperwork-feeling for a one-point formula change. It was the dullest stretch, and it just set up STAND collapsing.

diaries.fair: The ending card revealed a hidden ceiling and a party estimate I was never told, and said one choice at 43 removed my ceiling. diaries.again: I want to try keeping my head down and see whether the ceiling really moves, and to find out what the closed-case man was about.

best.what: Publicly conceding a correct Forum complaint and promising change. It felt like a real choice with stakes, and I kept waiting for it to come back.

worst.what: Pushing the bottom 20th yet again for the National Bonus. By then it was the same choice on repeat and nothing changed, and STAND just kept sliding.

skip.why: Same bottom 20th choice as Y41 and Y46, STAND dropped again, and I still had no idea what it meant.

diaries.fair: I reached Minister, kept integrity at 100 and exceeded both estimates, so it felt fair. It was a bit flat and anticlimactic, though, and the Y28 promise, the wet market clip, the chilli lady and the kueh man never paid off.
diaries.again: The middle decades were repetitive and several threads I was waiting on never came back. I'd want a break first, though the Declassified card made me curious about what a different path would show.

best.what: Writing down what everyone was really thinking at the Public Sector Transformation offsite. It felt like a bold, dramatic choice, though I never saw it pay off.

worst.what: The BTO flat year. I had no idea what BTO meant, so I picked the 'inside info' option blind and the game never explained it.

skip.why: There were only two years, so nothing was long enough to skip. The ending card was the flattest part, but it isn't a year.

diaries.fair: It ended at 24 after two taps, with no warning and no chance to recover. The card hints at a scholarship I never knew about, so I can't tell what I did wrong. A shock exit is fine in a game like this, but I'd want to understand why it happened.
diaries.again: Yes, mostly because it was over so quickly and I want to see what happens past year 2. I'm also curious what the scholarship thing means and whether the game has more to it than this.

skip.why: Single option, nothing happened, and the politics rumour just repeated without going anywhere.

skip.why: Walking every block for nine days, and then the same again in Y47. Repeated, low-stakes, and nothing much came of it that I could see.

diaries.again: The middle decades were too many single-option taps, and I'd want a break before trying again. The ceiling twist makes me curious, but not right now.

best.what: Told my Perm Sec everything about the journalist question and she said 'Thank you for coming to me'. A quiet payoff for being honest, and the one moment that felt like a person rather than a stat.

worst.what: The late years where every year was only option A: the same late-night/concert event repeated with no real choice, just watching STAND wobble and waiting for a politics invitation that never came.

skip.why: I asked about my ceiling and got no answer. It was a build-up to nothing, and it sat in the stretch where I had no choices anyway.

diaries.fair: I had 100 REP, 100 INTEG and 100 COMP and got retired as Perm Sec with no politics, no leak fallout and no Y17 crisis outcome. Lots of threads I was waiting on never paid off. The ceiling reveal was neat but arrived after it could matter.
diaries.again: The early and mid game had enough tension and I want to see the politics path, but I'd want more actual choices in the late years.

best.what: The Telegram leak, where I confessed 'It was you' and then the inquiry didn't find me. It was the one time a choice felt dangerous and dramatic.

worst.what: The Budget Round with only one choice and jargon like 'absorb' that I didn't understand. It was a tap-through year with no real decision.

skip.why: Refusing to blur the 31% utilisation figure was a dry spreadsheet moment, and the director stole my credit with no payoff I could see.

diaries.fair: I did everything the game hinted at, with 100 in three stats, and the politics invitation never came. It ended with a retirement card and no payoff for the Forum promises, the Y4 'game' comment or the 'different list'. It felt like it cut off before the story paid off.
diaries.again: Not right now. The middle years were slow and the threads I cared about never resolved, but I'd probably try again later for the politics route.

best.what: The Counter: telling them exactly why it would fail, which the ending card says removed my ceiling in the service. A blunt choice turning out to be the pivot of the whole life was the best twist, even though I only found out at the end.

worst.what: The repeat indicators choice (push the bottom 20th) and the repeat Polling Day walk. It was the same choice as Y41 and Y40 with the same shape, so it felt like grinding.

skip.why: Answering all five written PQs as if oral was a lot of reading about parliamentary procedure I had no context for, and nothing much came of it that I saw.

diaries.fair: I got to Minister with clean integrity, and the declassified reveal explained things I had wondered about for decades. It was a little disappointing that Cabinet hints never paid off.
diaries.again: It was 46 years of taps and the late years repeated themselves. I'd come back another day for the different path, not right now.

best.what: The Leak: I admitted it was me, and then waited years to see if the inquiry would catch up. It was the one choice that felt properly dangerous.

worst.what: A quiet year with only one option and STAND dropping for no reason I could see. Nothing to decide and nothing to read.

skip.why: Nothing happened, I got no choice, and I lost STAND with no explanation.

diaries.fair: I reached the top and retired, which is fine. But the threads I was waiting on (the MP, politics, the leak, my mother's pride) never paid off, and the card dropped a fact about something at age 85 that I'll never see. It felt like a lot of setup left hanging.
diaries.again: I enjoyed the ambition and the candour trade-off, but too many years were quiet with one option, and I'm not sure my choices change enough to justify another 38 years of tapping. Maybe later.

best.what: Telling them exactly why it would fail in The Counter. I only learned from the ending card that it removed my ceiling, so it was a good surprise in hindsight, though I didn't feel it at the time.

worst.what: The Committee of Supply, where I rebranded a scheme with a higher number. It was a dull dilemma with jargon I didn't follow, and it just cost me some INTEG.

skip.why: I asked about my ceiling and got no answer. It was a tease with no payoff, and I wanted something to happen.

diaries.fair: I reached the top grade, kept my integrity high and earned a lot, and the declassified card explained things clearly. I would have liked to see the Tea payoff and the Leak reveal. Neither seemed to land, which was a bit frustrating.
diaries.again: The ceiling reveal made me curious how different choices change the path, and I want to try for politics. But the middle years were slow, so I would be hoping for more happening.

best.what: The Y20 tender came back as a parliamentary question. I let the documentation speak, refused to ask a friend to hide it, and the Minister used my statement draft. This was the clearest case of an earlier choice paying off.

worst.what: I asked about my ceiling and it just cost me standing with no story attached. It felt like a trap with no payoff.

skip.why: The Budget Round haggling ended in 4 officers and half a system, which was a lot of numbers and not much drama. The ending card then undercut the consultancy choice I'd been waiting on.

diaries.fair: The reveal says one early honest choice removed my ceiling, but I never saw that happen or got a warning. It felt like the game hid the rule and then blamed me for it. The young officer who was supposed to become my boss never showed up, and the consultancy ending was a flat one-liner.
diaries.again: The hidden ceiling gives me something to chase, and I want to see if a different early choice changes the result. I'd probably play it on another break rather than right now.

best.what: The Counter: I told them exactly why the plan would fail, and the game later confirmed it raised my hidden ceiling to Deputy Secretary. Honesty paid off in a way I could see.

worst.what: Appraisal chat with only one option, and my standing fell despite outstanding appraisals. The late years gave me one button and no drama, so I was just tapping.

skip.why: One choice, STAND dropping for no clear reason, and nothing happening. It felt like filler right before the end.

diaries.fair: I got to the very top with full reputation, integrity and competence, so the result is fine. But so many threads I was told might come back never did, and the card's 'at 85 everything surfaces' is a threat for a life I will not get to play. It felt like it ended before the payoff.
diaries.again: Not right now. The early and mid career had good moments, but the last decade thinned out into single options. I would come back once I had a theory about how to trigger the callbacks.

best.what: Standing in the GRC team, winning 61.4% and becoming an MP. It was the first time the game swerved from a desk job into something dramatic, and the maiden speech choice felt personal.

worst.what: The ending card told me nothing I did mattered: the ceiling was fixed, the party had already decided, and no offer could have changed it. I picked the Board Seat for the drama and got a flat consultancy retirement at 38.

skip.why: Attending Meet-the-People Sessions weekly was a lot of tapping for very little happening. I only half understood what it was.

diaries.fair: Most of my threads never paid off: the tender COI, the leaker, the 'game' quote, the rebranded scheme and the backlash from resigning. Then the card says nothing could have changed the outcome. Choices are meant to be permanent and to come back, and that did not happen. I would have accepted a bad ending if it had come from something I did.
diaries.again: The ending soured it. I want to know my choices change something before I put in another 13 years. The early game had good moments, but I would want a hint that the ceiling is not fixed.

best.what: I published the raw cost-of-living feedback next to the Engagement Exercise report. It became the most-read government document and my REP finally moved, after years of fixing things nobody noticed.

worst.what: The General Election. I was railroaded into the team ticket, the single seat was locked behind a REP I did not have, and I lost at 48.2% with a line saying it was never about me. It felt like the game took the choice away.

skip.why: The quiet years of fixing unannounced processes (Y6-Y8) were the dullest stretch. Nothing happened and nobody noticed, and REP just sat there.

diaries.fair: The card says it was never about me, so a dozen years of choices ended in a vote I had almost no say in. A narrow loss at 48.2% feels cruel when the game made the key decision for me. The legacy lines were nice, though.
diaries.again: The run was short and I want to know whether the REP gate can be beaten. I also never saw the concert fallout and I'm curious whether it was ever going to come back.

best.what: Submitting to the pay committee under my own name and watching the formula get adjusted. It was the payoff for the Y23 Cabinet question and felt like my choices changed the system itself.

worst.what: The indicators choice for the third time in a row (bottom 20th). Same choice, same result, no new twist, and the bonus hint about rivals never paid off. It felt like a loop.

skip.why: Repeat of the indicators choice with only a hint that something would come of it. Nothing happened, so I'd have tapped through.

diaries.fair: I picked honest and ambitious options every time and got PM with integrity at 100, which matches. The declassified card explaining the ceiling and the Reshuffle was a nice reveal. I'd have liked some payoff for the Tuesday man though.
diaries.again: I enjoyed the pay committee arc, but the later decades repeated the same choices and many threads I set up went nowhere. I'd come back after a break to try the dishonest route, not right now.

best.what: Winning the seat with 53.1% and giving the maiden speech where I picked the thing I truly believed. It was a real risk and it felt like the climax of the climb.

worst.what: The background check. I disclosed everything and then nothing came of it, which was dull and let the air out of the tension the earlier choices had built.

skip.why: Choosing between a solo seat and a 'GRC team' meant nothing to me because the game never explained the term, so I was guessing on a big decision.

diaries.fair: I took the money and left politics, so retiring as a Parliamentary Secretary with a consultancy fits. The 'Minister' estimate on the card stung, and I wish I'd been told about it earlier.
diaries.again: The ending card showed me things I couldn't see while playing, like the ceiling, the party's estimate and the missed moment at 34, so I want to run it again knowing what to look for. The unpunished early choices annoyed me, though.

best.what: Awarding the tender to the genuinely better vendor, an ex-colleague, and having the paperwork look like a confession. It set up a real tension that I felt carried through the whole run.

worst.what: Running in the election and losing at 48.2%. The choice felt like it mattered, but the ending said it was never about me, so it felt like nothing I did counted.

skip.why: A new Reporting Officer arrived with loyalists and I just became indispensable on a file. It was office politics with little payoff and I do not remember it coming back.

diaries.fair: I made honest choices, my integrity went up to 69, and then the ending said it never mattered. Losing by under two points after all that, with no way to see what would have swung it, felt like the game shrugging at me. The 'very solid, nobody can remember an example' legacy line was funny though.
diaries.again: I want to know if the loss was avoidable. The game ended at 34 which felt short, and I would go in with different choices, but I am not sure I would put in much effort if the outcome is fixed.

best.what: The wet market walkabout where the chilli stallholder moment went viral. It was the first time a small, silly choice blew up into something that felt like it mattered.

worst.what: Conceding the third point on Facebook and watching STAND drop with no explanation. I couldn't tell what I'd done wrong, and being punished for honesty was just annoying to play.

skip.why: Not one specific year, but the stretch from Y33 to Y40 where I kept pushing the bottom 20th percentile for the bonus was the same loop over and over.

diaries.fair: I lost a seat after walking every block, with Integrity and Reputation at 100 and Competence at 86, and the card just says it was never about me. The game never taught me what did matter, and the PM ceiling went unused. It's a bit of a cheat to reveal the rules only at the end.
diaries.again: I'm annoyed enough to want to crack STAND, and the hidden ceiling and party estimate are a good mystery. I'd want a different early path first, though, because this one ran long.

best.what: The journalist reconstructing the leak story, and I told the Perm Sec everything first. His line that he'd never forget it was the one time a choice felt like it landed on a person.

worst.what: Town Council lift contract with the contractor's cousin. Picking the slow, proper option meant a dull admin loop, and it cost me REP for something I mostly just read about.

skip.why: Not one year in particular. The many single-option appraisal years blurred together, but they were short and I would have tapped through them anyway.

diaries.fair: The card says it never would have changed, which makes nine days of walking every block feel pointless. Losing is fine, but telling me after the fact that my choices couldn't matter takes the sting out of the story. I also never got the leak result I was told to wait eleven years for, and never saw the drawer letter come back.
diaries.again: I'd give it another go later. The slow middle of single-option years and the unresolved threads left me flat, and I want to know whether other lives actually pay anything off.

best.what: Asking Cabinet whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set themselves. It felt like a real stand against the system, and it set up the whole pay-formula theme that the ending card pays off.

worst.what: Another quiet year with only choice A: forty letters, kueh from the weekly man, nothing to decide. I was waiting for trouble and nothing came.

skip.why: Quiet year, one choice, fixed something nobody asked. Years 38 and 39 were both passive, so I would skip the pair, but 38 was first and set up a promise of trouble that never arrived.

diaries.fair: I always picked the honest route and ended at the top with integrity 100, which matches. But the ceiling reveal was a bit confusing: the 'party estimate' was Senior Minister of State and I beat it, so it felt like the game was telling me I overachieved without showing how.
diaries.again: I just spent 39 years tapping honest choices and the last stretch was quiet. I want a break, though the dishonest run tempts me later.

best.what: Walking every block every night for nine days in the election. The ending card then told me it raised my ceiling to Minister, so the big visible effort paid off in a way I could see.

worst.what: Another year with only one choice: answering five written PQs as if oral, with STAND dropping again and no reason given for being left off the Leadership Programme list. It felt like the game had stopped letting me play.

skip.why: Nothing I could decide, STAND fell again and I got a shrug of an event. It was the flattest stretch of a life that had been sagging for years.

diaries.fair: It was oddly fair because it explained the ceiling and the rumours, and it matched the pattern I suspected. It was also quietly cruel that nothing I did could change it for most of the run, and that I only learned the rules at the end.
diaries.again: The life was long and I played 46 years to learn the ceiling existed. I would want a break first, though I am curious enough that I would try again with the ending card in mind.

best.what: The background check found both my early sins, the leak and the fudged scheme number, and I disclosed everything. It felt like a real callback, and honesty paid off by raising INTEG.

worst.what: The Parliamentary Question year, where the only option was 'As usual: answer it straight'. I had no real choice, and the game had turned my own habit into a locked option.

skip.why: Nothing happened and I had one button. It was a forced tap, and STAND dropped anyway with no explanation.

diaries.fair: I reached the top, and the declassified card explained the key choice, the ceiling and the exposure number. The odd bit is that it says the hard ministry choice was at 52, while my notes put it around Y27-28. I couldn't square that.
diaries.again: I want to, but I'd need a break. A clean run to the top gave me few big surprises, and the late years felt flat and forced. A scandal run might be more fun later.

best.what: The kueh callback with the Tuesday man, the resident with the unreopenable case from Y13. Walking every block paid off in a small, human way.

worst.what: The indicators choice repeated for Y41-43. I picked the same option each time, nothing visibly changed except STAND dropping 2, and it felt like a chore.

skip.why: It was the third identical indicators choice in a row with the same small STAND penalty. Nothing new happened.

diaries.fair: I reached DPM with 100 integrity, so the result was fine, but the game hid the one mechanic that mattered for 45 years and then revealed it on the final card. My honest streak seemingly did nothing, and the lift audit, my daughter and the board seat never paid off. That felt like a trick, not a twist.
diaries.again: The slow stretches were long and the mechanic only made sense at the end. I'd try a shadier run another day, not now.

best.what: The maiden speech, where I said the one thing I truly believe, and then got a note from a Minister I'd never met saying 'That needed saying.' It was the one point where the honesty felt like it was building to something.

worst.what: Walking every block for nine nights, then losing at 48.2% with a card telling me it was never going to be about me anyway. All that effort and the result felt decided before I tapped.

skip.why: The tea-as-vetting stretch was slow and full of terms I didn't know. I had to guess what was happening until the disappointed man showed up.

diaries.fair: The loss felt imposed. I walked every block as a choice and the card basically said it didn't matter, so my choice was pointless. Also the 'it was never going to be about you' line felt like the game telling me my agency was fake. The declassified file was great, though.
diaries.again: I want to see the other side of that Y31 fork. The declassified card made me curious what a less honest run looks like, and it is only a short life.

best.what: Background check found both my early leak and the rebrand, I disclosed everything, and got promoted anyway. The first time a choice came back and rewarded honesty, which hooked me.

worst.what: STAND dropped again and again (42 down to 22) despite outstanding appraisals and maxed stats, and I could not tell why or do anything about it. It felt like pressing buttons with no effect.

skip.why: One of the long STAND-decline years where I answered PQs, campaigned straight and watched the number fall with no new information. Nothing happened except a number.

diaries.fair: The declassified card explained a lot, such as the repeated 'steady' wording, and made the stalling make sense. I still would have liked to see the ceiling earlier, because I spent decades not knowing what I was playing against.
diaries.again: The ending card showed hidden systems I didn't know I was playing against, so I want a second run using what I now know. I'd want more happening in the middle years, though.

best.what: The think tank paper built on my raw feedback got cited by both sides in Parliament and I jumped to Deputy Secretary. A small choice from earlier blew up into something big.

worst.what: The General Election. I picked the single seat without knowing what GRC meant, and the game just told me I lost at 48.2%. I had no idea what I'd done wrong and no way to affect it.

skip.why: Reporting 31% utilisation with a recovery plan was all jargon and spreadsheet-feeling, with no drama and no idea what it meant.

diaries.fair: I played a clean, honest career and then one choice I couldn't understand ended everything. The card says it was never about me, which makes my choices feel pointless. The director who stole my slides never came back either, which was a letdown.
diaries.again: The consequences-come-back structure hooked me and I want to see what the other election choice does. But I'd want it to explain terms first.

best.what: My Perm Sec said 'Thank you for coming to me' after I confessed the IMC leak first, and the matter was closed. It was the one time an early choice paid off in a way I could feel.

worst.what: The ending. I took the consultancy offer and the game just stopped at 33 with a flat card. I never got the politics invitation I was building towards.

skip.why: Deputy Secretary and running the ministry transition were all grades and acronyms I didn't understand. Nothing dramatic happened and I only remember the stats shifting.

diaries.fair: I left by choice, but it felt abrupt and I didn't know it was the last year. The lunch speeches being about the scheme and not me was a good sting, but the daughter fallout from Y4 never showed up, and I was waiting for it.
diaries.again: The slow-burn callbacks hooked me and I want to see what happens with a different choice on the leak. I'd want clearer signposts for what the grades and stats mean first.

best.what: Asked for the hard ministry nobody wants, got a big STAND boost and became Deputy PM. It was the one time the honest, ambitious choice paid off visibly.

worst.what: Picking the Indicators option B yet again. By the fifth time it was the same choice with the same small stat shuffle, and I was just tapping.

skip.why: Not being on the Leadership Programme list was just a flat result with no explanation, and it felt like the game quietly closing a door on me.

diaries.fair: Perfect integrity and top scores ended at DPM with 'your ceiling refused it', and I never got a clear way to see or change that. The ending card explained it after the fact, which is cool but felt unfair as I played. I never got to try for PM knowingly.
diaries.again: I'd like to try for PM, but 46 years of mostly identical choices is a lot. I'd come back after a break, and only if I could skip quickly through the quiet years.

best.what: Publishing the raw cost-of-living feedback as Deputy Secretary at MOE. It felt like a proper gamble and moved my REP and INTEG a lot.

worst.what: Standing in the GRC election and losing at 48.2%. I picked it because it looked dramatic, but it was a single pick with no real decision after it, and the ending card said it was never about me anyway.

skip.why: Running the reorg transition was administrative and I barely remember anything about it. It did not seem to matter later.

diaries.fair: I lost by under two points after one choice and then was retired at 34 with no say. The 'it was never about you' line stung. The Y8 background-check honesty seemed to count for nothing, and the legacy line was funny but felt like a shrug.
diaries.again: The leak callback hooked me and I want to see what a higher REP run does. The run was short, so another go is quick, but I would want more choices in the later years.
